content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to use a relational module to modulate the latent space learnt by an adversarial AE. The relational module utilize a small subset of labelled data to minimize a relational loss that encourages parts of the latent code to be mapped by relational latent operators.
content.main_review:
Pros:
1. The paper is written fluently and effectively convey the authors' ideas in a concise way.
2. The proposed Rel-Learner seems an interesting way to encourage weak disentanglement. I think this is relatively novel.
3. The evaluation is thorough. Experiments demonstrate the advantage of the proposed methods in terms of clustering accuracy, disentanglement measurement and relational accuracy.

Cons:
1. There are constraints imposed in the method that makes it not very applicable to more real-world datasets. For example, the authors restrict the latent factors can only take discrete values, and state that each combination of latent factors is a mode in the mixture of gaussian.  First of all, the method is going to have scalability issues once more factors are included. Secondly, most of the data generating factors in real world are real-valued. I have concerns about how can the proposed module be extended to such cases. I think the authors could discuss more on this issue.
2. Another constraint is that a set of valid relations between ground-truth latent factors need to be determined for each different dataset. For the proposed synthetic datasets, the required work is not so onerous. However for real-world cases, where relations are far less-well defined, and sometimes not binary, how can the model be adapted to be useful in this scenario?
content.summary_of_the_review: A technically sound, relatively novel paper with proper evaluations. The paper fall shorts in discussing some of the constraints imposed, and the method's adaptability to more real-world cases.

display_title: Official Review of Paper3080 by Reviewer UkzY

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new objective for training VAEs with disentangled representations. There are some experiments to show that the new objective learn disentangled representations.
content.main_review:
While the paper has promise, it has some shortcomings that need to be addressed/clarified before I can give a higher recommendation. 

I don’t see the difference between prior and meta-prior. I think what this paper calls ‘meta-prior’ is no different from a typical prior? 

The novelty seems rather limited, as the encoder and decoder are learned by a fairly standard adversarial autoencoder objective with a Gaussian mixture prior. The main novelty seems to be the relational learner, but I have some concerns about it:

First, how does the relational learner affect the encoder and decoder? If I change the relational network, does that affect how I train the decoder and encoder? From Eq.(1) it seems that the answer is no, then it’s unclear how the relational network benefits encoder and decoder training. 

Second, learning the relational network requires paired data, the samples need to be paired in a specific way. I don’t understand how this can be done with any dataset that’s not synthetic, where you already know the correct disentangled factors. A similar shortcoming is that relational learning requires knowledge of f, which characterizes how different data modes are related to each other. Naturally, given the synthetic dataset we can design f, but given a non-synthetic real-world dataset, how should practitioners design the function f? 

It seems that the prior p(z) is estimated from labeled data? However, I do not quite understand how the prior is learned based on the description in the paper. In section 4.1 (which the paper promises an explanation) the only relevant information seems to be the number of distinct modes? How do you construct a prior given the number of distinct modes? In practice, the number of modes is probably unavailable, as real datasets probably do not have a small number of distinct modes, and even if it does, the number of modes is probably not known. 

The proposed method requires additional supervision (as described above), while I do not think the compared baselines (such as beta-VAE and factorVAE) require such additional supervision, so how do you ensure that the comparison is fair?
content.summary_of_the_review: I think the paper works on an interesting problem, but there are many flaws that needs to be addressed before I can recommend acceptance.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.title: Response to Review #2
content.comment:
**I don’t see the difference between prior and meta-prior. [...]**

We call p(z) “meta-prior” in order to reflect its conceptual role according to the notion of meta-priors introduced by (Bengio et al., 2013). From a purely statistical point of view, p(z) is indeed the prior distribution of the model. We will uniform the terminology in the revised version, if it helps to improve the overall readability of the paper.

**[...]First, how does the relational learner affect the encoder and decoder? [...]**

The benefit is mostly the other way around, i.e. the relational learner is benefitting from working in a structured latent space (learned by the AbsAE) rather than learning relations from unstructured data. This way, the ReL does not have to care about the perceptual part of the task, it only needs to learn how to relate different latent codes with each other. The encoder and decoder will then make sure that the latent codes actually contain the relevant low-level perceptual information needed for getting accurate reconstructions. This makes the ReL agnostic to the specific dataset that is used, letting it focus only on how to relate the different Gaussians of the prior.

**Second, learning the relational network requires paired data, the samples need to be paired in a specific way. [...]. A similar shortcoming is that relational learning requires knowledge of f, which characterizes how different data modes are related to each other. [...]**

We partly addressed this concern in points 4. and 5. of  the general comment, but we would like to elaborate a bit further on that here. 

In order to construct a training tuple for the ReL, it is needed a small set of samples labelled to identify relevant combinations of factors in the data that serve to build the AbsAE prior (e.g. in the case of a dataset composed of images of different vehicles, where we want to learn the “change_colour” relation, we may desire to collect labelles samples corresponding to the concepts “red vehicles”, “yellow vehicles”, “green vehicles”, etc. and then construct the prior components in the regions of the latent space where the labelled samples end up being encoded. If the relation of interest is “change_category”, we collect samples of “motorbikes”, “automobiles”, “trucks”, etc. If we care about both colours and categories, the relevant combinations of factors will be “red motorbike”, “green motorbike”, “yellow trucks”, and so on). The training tuples of eq. 9 do not leverage additional labelled data. Instead, the latent codes are sampled from the appropriate gaussian prior (which, by construction, identifies the corresponding concept in the data space). It is then the responsibility of the AbsAE to make sure that the gaussian actually corresponds to a specific combination of factors, but the ReL is agnostic to that. 

The f function is defined over the abstract concepts. Using the previous example, a possible “change colour” function can be designed in this way:
change_colour(green_vehicles) = red_vehicles
change_colour(red_vehicles) = yellow_vehicles
change_colour(yellow_vehicles) = green_vehicles
Please note that this definition is agnostic to the fact that the data samples are either real-world or synthetic. As long as we can “connect” each symbolic concept appearing in the domain and codomain of this function  with a component of p(z), the ReL is, in principle, able to  learn the relation.

**It seems that the prior p(z) is estimated from labeled data? However, I do not quite understand how the prior is learned based on the description in the paper. [...]**

We empirically estimate the means and covariances of the gaussian components of p(z) from a small set of data labelled with ancillary information that describe relevant data properties/factors. We do not seek to model the actual modes in the input samples. While this gives only an approximation of the actual shape of the relevant region of the latent space, during training the encoder will be encouraged to adapt to such learned prior. We explain this part right after equation 6. We will try to explain this part more in detail in the revised version of this paper. As for the number of modes, there is no need to encode all possible combinations of generative factors into the prior components. Some factors could not be interesting and therefore considered as nuisances. For example, for the Shapes 3D dataset the “floor color” and “wall color” factors are treated as nuisances, so the different gaussians of p(z) will encode different floor and wall colours images.

**The proposed method requires additional supervision (as described above), while I do not think the compared baselines (such as beta-VAE and factorVAE) require such additional supervision, so how do you ensure that the comparison is fair?**

We addressed this in point 2 of  the general comment.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper deals with a weak disentanglement problem. In conventional disentanglement setups, different generative factors are assumed to be encoded to different dimensions. However, weak disentanglement in this paper assumes a specific combination of generative factors is encoded to a certain region in the latent space.
To this end, the authors propose a generative model based on VAE. This new method has 2 components: an abstraction autoencoder (AbsAE) and a relational learner (ReL). AbsAE is basically an adversarial autoencoder. ReL models the relations among different regions in the latent space.
In the first stage, the model trains AbsAE following a standard optimization of an adversarial autoencoder. Then for each kind of combination of generative factors, 20 (or more) samples are provided. Then for each 20 samples, they are used to estimate a Gaussian in the latent space to form a subspace for this kind of factor combination. Then in the second stage, the authors construct (input, relation, output) training samples for latent codes. Then the ReL learns how to perform changes to the latent codes from one region to another. 
The authors illustrate the proposed model's performance on 3 datasets: HWF, dSprites, and Shapes3D. Both qualitative and quantitative results are provided.
content.main_review:
Pros:
1. I generally agree with the motivations proposed in this paper. Separating relevant factors of variations of the data in single isolated dimensions of the latent representations is indeed too restrictive. Also, based on (Locatello et al, 2019), weak supervision (and inductive biases) could help disentanglement.
2. The illustrations (text and fig) of the method is clear in general. I can follow the paper without major confusions.
3. Various experiments are performed. The goals of the experiments are also clearly listed upfront. Both qualitative and quantitative results are provided. Sensitivity studies on the parameters are also included in the paper.
4. I think some experimental scenarios are interesting, e.g. HWF.

Cons:
1. It seems that each combination of generative factors requires certain amount of labeled samples (e.g. 20). Though the authors claim this is weak-supervision, the number of labeled samples could go up quickly. For instance, 3 factors each with 10 discrete values ($10^3=1000$), or 10 factors each with 2 values ($2^{10}=1024$). You might need tens of thousands of labeled samples. This limits the generality of the model.
2. I'm not sure why authors choose 20 or 30 samples for Gaussian estimation. Maybe an additional experiment on the number of samples would make the claims more convincing.
3. If the generative factor is continuous, how would your model handle such case?
4. In HWF, how you model the case `6+8=14`, `6-8=-2`? I guess your model might not handle such cases?
5. It seems that the relation learner really depends on the specific scenario. One needs to design domain-specific relation learner. This issue makes the paper a bit less general.
6. In sec 3.1, $y_{g_i}$ should be explained.
7. I think Eq. 9 actually requires extra supervision (e.g. how the inputs "relate" to the output)?
8. Given that you used some extra supervision, is it a bit unfair to compare with unsupervised $\beta$-VAE or FactorVAE?
9. Though I generally agree dimension-wise disentanglement is indeed too restrictive, besides relaxing the problem to the weak disentanglement, you can also relax the problem to group-wise disentanglement [1,2]. It is worth discussing and comparing.

[1] Bai, J., Wang, W. and Gomes, C.. Contrastively Disentangled Sequential Variational Autoencoder. NeurIPS 2021.
[2] Hosoya, H.. Group-based Learning of Disentangled Representations with Generalizability for Novel Contents. IJCAI 2019.
content.summary_of_the_review: In general, the idea introduced in this paper is interesting and inspiring. The whole paper is also written clearly and well-organized. The combination of AbsAE and ReL is novel. In the experiments, the goals are clearly listed. However, the problem setup is still a bit too ideal. The so-called weak-supervision may not be that weak when the number of combinations grows. Also, the datasets are all synthetic and whether the relation learner can generalize to other domains is not clear. If authors can show some results on more real-world and less well-designed scenarios, the claims would be more convincing.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Response to Review #1
content.comment:
**It seems that each combination of generative factors requires certain amount of labeled samples (e.g. 20). [...] This limits the generality of the model.**

Apart from our response point 1 in the general comment, we would like to add that it is not needed to encode all possible combinations of factors into the latent space, but only the ones that are relevant for the relations.

**I'm not sure why authors choose 20 or 30 samples for Gaussian estimation.**

We empirically found that these were the numbers that allowed us to estimate the initial prior gaussians in a stable and reliable way. While a higher number seems to not provide a significant improvement, a lower number can result in a bad estimation of the gaussian’s parameter (e.g. when some labelled samples are not the most representative for the specific entity), making for the encoder hard to correctly fit the data samples into the estimated prior Gaussian. We are expanding Table 1 with an ablation study on this aspect.

**In HWF, how you model the case 6+8=14, 6-8=-2?**

The ReL can easily account for that (needs only to add one latent code for the sign). In the paper we show that the ReL can have different number of inputs, depending on the arity of the relations to be learned (e.g. HWF has binary relations, while dSprites and Shapes3D use unary relations). We thank the reviewer for the suggestion, we add more qualitative examples in the revised appendix to better show the flexibility of the ReL.

**It seems that the relation learner really depends on the specific scenario. One needs to design domain-specific relation learner.**

See point 3 of the general comment.

**In sec 3.1, ygi should be explained.**

Thank you for the comment, we will include an explanation of y_{g_i} in the revised version.

**Though I generally agree dimension-wise disentanglement is indeed too restrictive, besides relaxing the problem to the weak disentanglement, you can also relax the problem to group-wise disentanglement [1,2] [...].**

We thank the reviewer for the suggestions. 

In [1], the authors disentangle representation of sequential data into “static” factors, that are constant along all the duration of the sequence, and “dynamic” factors, that vary across the timesteps. They apply their method on synthetic benchmarks. Their work is focused on sequential data, and does not explicitly leverage relational information (except from the implicit temporal relation induced by the sequences).

As for [2], the authors separate the latent space into group-common “content” variables and instance-specific “transformation” variables. A standard gaussian prior is imposed on the two parts of the representation. The result is strong disentanglement between the contents and transformation factors.

Both works perform controlled manipulation of latent codes at a sub-symbolic level, i.e. by swapping the different parts of the representations between different encoded samples. This requires knowledge of both the content and the transformations in the samples in order for the desired manipulation to be carried out effectively.

In general, it seems that these works, while presenting interesting ideas, stem from the notion of strong disentanglement and then relax it in order to get a certain type of more flexible weak disentanglement. On the other hand, in our work we show an orthogonal approach: we start from a relational learning perspective, and show that by integrating relational information into the neural model we can get weak disentanglement almost as a (very useful) byproduct.

We will add these considerations (in compatibility with the page limit) in the final version of the paper.

content.title: Further reviews of authors' response
content.comment:
The following ordering is based on my original review points in "Cons".
1. First, prior works containing the same limitations does not mean we as reviewers should accept such limitations for this paper. Good papers should improve over the previous limitations. Second, you mentioned "we already recognize this and outline a possible way forward to address it". Future outlines/blueprints do not count towards the contributions of this paper. I would be convinced only If you concretely prove such ideas through methods and experiments. While you mentioned several potential merits of your method, the experiments are not that strong enough to support such claims. All used datasets are really well-defined and well-constructed. Third, regarding "it is not needed to encode all ... but only ...", you need experiments to support your claims. Also, even if some combinations of factors do not show up in your training set, it doesn't mean it will not exist in the test set. 
2. Thx for the clarification. But I'm still concerned that such number of samples needed is application-dependent. You might need more for other domains and extra effort to tune this number. This would make the method hard to generalize easily.
3. I think your response for this point is "e.g. continuous factors could be encoded using a uniform prior instead of a GM". Again, unless you show concrete experiments, I could not be convinced by such high-level claims.
4. You mentioned you can add a sign symbol to account for negative. I'm not sure then how do you handle two digits. 14 has 2 digits "1" and "4". If you claim the ReL can handle it well by adding extra sth, then the ReL itself is providing quite strong supervision already. If ReL is designed to handle all details like a blackbox, then it is a quite strong supervision.
5. If you claim your ReL is general simply because ReL reads inputs and output a latent code, acting as a general framework, then it is not convincing. In this sense, ReL acts like a black box and tells you all the relations in the hidden space. It is not that different from giving the whole relations in the input space, which is almost fully supervised. Providing supervision to the latent space doesn't mean it is then weak supervision.
6. Pls do.
7. I assume your response is point 5 from "general response". While I understand "statistical relational learning" might allow relation tuples, it is then no longer "weak supervision". For instance, 6+8=14, how would you construct the latent space for 14? 66+74=140, how would you model 140? The number of latent space can go crazy easily. If you only play with single-digit scenarios, then the work's significance is really limited.
8. I'm not sure if  [Locatello et al, 2019] and [Gabbay et al. 2021] receive the same supervision as yours.
9. As I mentioned in point 4, ReL is providing strong relation supervisions. This is also a "controlled manipulation" with supervision. But I agree you did take an orthogonal direction for your paper. The key issue is that I'm convinced by those papers, the supervision is weak, but I believe your supervision is much stronger and hard to generalize well (see previous points).

content.title: Reviews' general comment (1\2)
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewers for their insightful comments and suggestions. We are preparing a revised version of the paper in order to take into account the revisions, and we welcome very much interaction and any further comments which can support and guide us towards uploading a satisfactory revision by the end of the rebuttal period. In this general comment, we provide some general clarifications that might be of interest to all reviewers.  Reviewer-specific concerns are addressed in separate comments. 

1. **The amount of supervision required could go up quickly when there are many generative factors, or when the factors can take up many possible values. / The model has trouble handling continuous generative factors.**

We agree with the reviewers that these are indeed key constraints of our model. Please note that while the amount of supervision increases w.r.t the number of factors, but not w.r.t the number of relations. Furthermore, many works in the literature are known to potentially suffer from similar issues (even if sometimes the supervision is given implicitly) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].
In the conclusions, we already recognize this and outline a possible way forward to address it, i.e. encoding the values of each generative factor in separate latent spaces. This could solve the problem of the combinatorial escalation of prior components, as well as provide more flexibility for encoding different types of generative factors in the most appropriate way (e.g. continuous factors could be encoded using a uniform prior instead of a GM). These further developments aside, we believe that our work can still contribute significantly to the discussion in the research community, by setting a new perspective on the disentanglement problem, while not providing a definitive answer to that (as it is often the case in initial works). 

*References*

[1]. Tao, Y., Takagi, K., & Nakata, K. (2021). Clustering-friendly Representation Learning via Instance Discrimination and Feature Decorrelation. ICLR2021.

[2]. Hristov, Y., & Ramamoorthy, S. (2020). Learning from Demonstration with Weakly Supervised Disentanglement. ICLR2021.

[3]. Chen, J., & Batmanghelich, K. (2020, April). Weakly supervised disentanglement by pairwise similarities. In Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (Vol. 34, No. 04, pp. 3495-3502).

[4]. Zheng, M., Wang, F., You, S., Qian, C., Zhang, C., Wang, X., & Xu, C. (2021). Weakly Supervised Contrastive Learning. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (pp. 10042-10051).

[5]. Xu, Y., Qian, Q., Li, H., Jin, R., & Hu, J. (2021). Weakly Supervised Representation Learning With Coarse Labels. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (pp. 10593-10601).


2. **It is unfair to compare a semi-supervised model with the unsupervised \beta-VAE and FactorVAE models.**

While we agree that comparing a semi-supervised method with an unsupervised method is not fair in terms of disentanglement performance, the main goal of Figure 3 was to show that our model can increase the amount of disentanglement regularization without affecting the reconstruction performance. We use beta-VAE and FactorVAE to provide a baseline for the reconstruction accuracy. We know we can expect that they can increase disentanglement only at the expense of reconstruction, while our model is much more stable in that aspect. In the revision, we will make this clearer. The direct comparison of the disentanglement performance of the models is presented in Table 3, where we compare our model with the two recent semi-supervised methods of [Locatello et al, 2019] and [Gabbay et al. 2021], and this in our opinion is a fair and relevant comparison. 

3. **The ReL is domain-specific.**

While the relevant entities and relations are different for each dataset (as we think it is natural), the architecture of the ReL is general. We used exactly the same architecture of the ReL for the dSprites and Shapes3D datasets, while for HWF we had only to increase the input size of the network, (since we were learning binary relations instead of unary ones), resulting in a negligible difference in terms of computational performance.

content.title: Reviews' general comment (2\2)
content.comment:
4. **The ReL can only work with synthetic datasets.**

We do not think that the ReL is affected much by the use of real-world data. Real-world datasets increase the burden on the perceptual part of the network (i.e. the AbsAE) as it is more difficult to effectively encode the information needed for reconstructing the original data sample. As long as we have access to the supervised information needed to construct the prior p(z), the ReL is able to learn relations among the prior gaussians, regardless of the specific perceptual information encoded in the latent codes. In the case of real-world data, the relevant factors will manifest themselves in a noisy way, but this can be taken into account by the prior, since the gaussian component are meant to model the uncertainty of the real-world manifestation of factors values (this is also why we perform data augmentation on our data by corrupting the data samples in various ways).

5.**The construction of the training tuples of Eq. 9 requires extra supervision.**

We assume that each dataset is composed of the real-world manifestations of a set of entities that can be related to each other by some relations. Both the relevant entities and relations are prior knowledge (they could be extracted, for example, from a knowledge graph or an ontology). However, we consider this an “ontological-level supervision”, as entities and relations are only specified in a symbolic way (i.e. through the f function), not as typical sample-level annotations (so there is no actual “extra supervision” needed in data).
We note that this is a common setting in statistical relational learning, where it is assumed to have a set of (head, relation, tail) tuples to characterize the relations to be learned. In our work, however, the relations are specified only through the f function. Our aim is to “embed” such symbolic ontological knowledge into the model in order to perform changes to the relevant entities. Weak disentanglement is a consequence of the successful embedding of this knowledge. One advantage of our approach is that we are thus able to construct new relational tuples by reifying the symbolic relation “on-demand” and in a “data-free” fashion, i.e. by directly sampling the latent space, instead of relying on an additional dataset of annotated relational data.
